quartiers:The Old Town.name: The Old Town
quartiers:The Old Town.teaser: One limestone street, five squares and the side lanes where Dubrovnik still eats: time it against the ships
quartiers:The Old Town.story: Walk in at Pile and the Stradun pulls you straight to Ploče, its paving polished by centuries of shoes until it shines after rain and turns slick underfoot. The life is off to the sides. Luža square gathers the Sponza, St Blaise and the bell tower; Gundulić square has its morning stalls under the poet's statue; Poljana Boškovića sits at the foot of the Jesuit Stairs. Climb the narrow lanes, Antuninska, Boškovićeva, Palmotićeva, and the menus shrink to one language. Up on Prijeko the touts work the tables. In late October the cruise traffic is thinning, but on a two-ship day the town still fills from mid-morning.
quartiers:The Old Town.why: Come before nine or after half past six, and turn uphill off the Stradun for every meal.
facts: The Stradun, the squares of Luža, Gundulić and Poljana Boškovića, and the stepped side lanes
Before 9am or after 6.30pm; Dubrovnik caps cruise calls at two ships a day, but those days still crowd the middle hours (Oct 2026)
The morning stalls on Gundulićeva Poljana, then the climb up the Jesuit Stairs
Proto, Kopun, Buffet Škola, Barba, Taj Mahal, D'vino for a glass; Lady Pi-Pi and Stara Loža at the top of town; Restaurant 360 closes from November to late March

sources.label: Croatia Week — Dubrovnik moves against overtourism (two cruise calls a day)

quartiers:Pile.name: Pile
quartiers:Pile.teaser: Every taxi, coach and bus ends at Pile: cross the drawbridge, or turn left for the fort on its rock
quartiers:Pile.story: Pile is the land door of the city and it still behaves like one: buses swinging round the stop, coach groups gathering under a guide's paddle, taxis idling by the moat garden. Above the outer gate the drawbridge chains still hang; St Blaise stands in his niche over the arch. Step through and Onofrio's great fountain is the first thing you meet. Outside, Brsalje runs to the terrace of Nautika in the old Nautical School, and a path drops to Kolorina cove and climbs to Lovrijenac on its rock. This is also where you catch the bus out to Gruž and Lapad.
quartiers:Pile.why: Sit on Brsalje at dusk, with Bokar on one side and Lovrijenac on the other, before you go in.
facts: Pile Gate and its drawbridge, Brsalje's sea terrace and the path to Lovrijenac
Early morning, before the coach groups arrive, or at sunset from Brsalje
The Libertas bus booth at the gate: lines 1A and 1B run to Gruž, 4 and 6 to Lapad and Babin Kuk; about EUR 1.73 at the kiosk, EUR 2.50 on board (Oct 2026)
Nautika (Brsalje 3) for the formal dinner; for supplies, the Konzum supermarket is a few minutes inside, on Gundulićeva Poljana

quartiers:Ploče.name: Ploče
quartiers:Ploče.teaser: Out through Ploče Gate: the old quarantine halls, a town beach and the best view back at the walls
quartiers:Ploče.story: Ploče is where the city faced east, towards the caravan roads and the plague that rode them. Cross the bridge from the Revelin and the road runs past the long stone halls of Lazareti, then drops to Banje beach with the walls and Lokrum in the same frame. Above the road the cable car's lower station sends cabins up Srđ. Further on, the grand hotels stand along Frana Supila looking back at the town, and up Hvarska locals queue at Pizzeria Tabasco. At night, with the walls lit gold across the water, this is the side to sit on.
quartiers:Ploče.why: Eat outside here on a summer night: you get the floodlit walls without the Stradun prices.
facts: Lazareti, Banje beach, the cable car up Srđ and the view back over the old port
After dark, when the walls are lit
The walk from Ploče Gate past Lazareti to Banje, with the old port below you
Pizzeria Tabasco (Hvarska 48a); book the terrace in July and August

quartiers:Gruž.name: Gruž
quartiers:Gruž.teaser: Where the ferries, the cruise ships and the morning fish all come in: Dubrovnik's working front door by sea
quartiers:Gruž.story: Gruž is the Dubrovnik that works for a living. Ferries for the Elaphiti and the coast load at the long quay, cruise ships tie up at the terminal and dwarf the stone houses, and at half past six the boats bring the fish to the market on Obala Stjepana Radića. Note that the ACI marina is not here: it sits about five kilometres further up the Rijeka Dubrovačka, at Komolac, where the inlet narrows. From Gruž, buses 1A and 1B reach Pile in a quarter of an hour or so. Go early, buy, have a coffee by the water, and you are back before the Old Town wakes.
quartiers:Gruž.why: Be at the market before nine: by ten the fish is gone and the quay belongs to the cruise coaches.
facts: The market, the ferry quay for the Elaphiti, and the harbour front of Obala Stjepana Radića
The fish hall first, then the produce stalls; bring cash in small notes
Gruž Market for the provisions; coffee at Cogito Coffee (its own card) on the quay

quartiers:Lapad.name: Lapad
quartiers:Lapad.teaser: Pine woods, a family bay and a car-free strip: where Dubrovnik lives when the Old Town is full
quartiers:Lapad.story: Lapad is the peninsula of hotels and flats west of Gruž, and it is where the city goes to swim and stroll. The pedestrian Šetalište kralja Zvonimira runs down under its plane trees to the beach in Uvala Lapad, lined with cafés where grandparents and students share the benches. Behind it rises Petka, a pine and holm-oak forest park of about 192 metres, with paths up to views of the Elaphiti; Babin Kuk spreads its hotels at the far end. Konoba Atlantic Kitchen feeds the residents, and the Asia Shop on Iva Vojnovića solves a galley's soy and nori problems.
quartiers:Lapad.why: Walk up Petka in the late afternoon and come down to eat in Lapad, not in the walls.
facts: Uvala Lapad beach, the pedestrian Šetalište kralja Zvonimira and the paths of Petka hill
Late afternoon into the evening walk; quieter from November, when many hotels close or slow down (check the season)
The climb up Petka for the view over the Elaphiti; Babin Kuk's shore path is the gentler alternative
Konoba Atlantic Kitchen (Kardinala Alojzija Stepinca 42); book the small terrace a few days ahead

curiosities:A ruler for one month.name: A ruler for one month
curiosities:A ruler for one month.teaser: The Republic of Ragusa feared one man more than any fleet, so it gave its head of state a month
curiosities:A ruler for one month.story: For four and a half centuries, from the Treaty of Zadar in 1358 to Marmont's decree of 1808, Ragusa ran itself on suspicion of ambition. Every noble entered the Major Council at eighteen; it chose a Senate of patricians over forty, the standard count is 45, for a year at a time; a seven-member Minor Council handled the day. On top sat a Rector who served exactly one month, had to wait two years before he could stand again, and lived shut inside his palace for the whole term, leaving it only on state business. Nobody was meant to get used to power.
curiosities:A ruler for one month.why: It explains the whole city: a merchant aristocracy that trusted no single man, and kept its independence that way.
facts: Stand in the atrium of the Rector's Palace (its own card is under Culture) and look up at the rooms he could not leave
The Senate's size and the Major Council's entry age changed over the centuries; 45 senators and about 300 nobles are the usual figures, not fixed ones

curiosities:The wind that excused a crim.name: The wind that excused a crime
curiosities:The wind that excused a crim.teaser: Dubrovnik swears its old Senate stopped work when the jugo blew: a lovely story with no paper behind it
curiosities:The wind that excused a crim.story: The jugo comes up from the south-east, warm and wet, piling the sea against the rocks below the walls and pressing on the head like a hand. Dubrovnik tells a story about it: that the Republic's councils would not sit or pass sentence while it blew, and that a crime done in a hard jugo earned a lighter penalty, because the wind was known to unsettle judgement. Travel writers repeat it as law. Look for the statute, though, and it is not there: the story lives in folklore collections and guidebooks, not in any archive anyone cites. People still blame the jugo for headaches and short tempers.
curiosities:The wind that excused a crim.why: Treat it as what Dubrovnik feels about its weather, not as Republic law.
facts: Walk out to the rocks at Pile or Ploče on a jugo day in autumn or winter and watch the swell break against the walls
The Senate and leniency claims appear only in popular and folklore sources (e.g. the USC folklore archive, Total Croatia News); no Republic statute or Senate record is cited for them

sources.label: Total Croatia News — Not feeling well today? Blame it on the jugo

curiosities:Why every façade matches.name: Why every façade matches
curiosities:Why every façade matches.teaser: The Stradun looks designed in one go because, after 1667, it was: a rebuild run by rule from Rome
curiosities:Why every façade matches.story: On the morning of 6 April 1667 the ground shook for a few seconds and the medieval city came down; fires burned for days after. The Rector was among the dead. The man who saved the shape of the place never saw it: Stjepan Gradić, a Ragusan priest who ran the Vatican Library, lobbied the Pope and Europe's courts for money and pressed the Senate to rebuild rather than move. What rose was Baroque and regulated: the Stradun's houses at one height, shops below with the door and the counter window under a single arch, flats above. That sameness is policy, not chance.
curiosities:Why every façade matches.why: Look at the ground floors: the door-and-counter arches repeat, house after house.
facts: Walk the Stradun and count the matching shop arches; the Sponza is one of the few buildings that came through the quake (its own card)
The death toll: Robin Harris counts about 2,000 inside the walls, older sources up to 5,000; the magnitude (about 7) is a modern estimate

curiosities:Marin Držić.name: Marin Držić
curiosities:Marin Držić.teaser: The Renaissance comic who mocked Dubrovnik's grandees, and later plotted to overthrow them
curiosities:Marin Držić.story: Marin Držić was born in the city in 1508, trained as a priest, and spent his life broke, restless and very funny. His Dundo Maroje, first staged in 1551, sends a miser to Rome after his spendthrift son and lets the servant Pomet run rings round everyone: Croatian theatre still starts there, and the Summer Festival keeps staging it. Late in life he wrote to the Medici in Florence asking for help to topple the patrician government that had laughed at his plays. Nothing came of it. He died in Venice in 1567. His house on Široka is now a small museum of his stage world.
curiosities:Marin Držić.why: See a Držić play in Croatian if one is on: you will follow Pomet without a word of the language.
facts: The House of Marin Držić, Široka 7; the capon dish at Kopun on Poljana Boškovića (its own card)
curiosities:Marin Držić.maps_query: House of Marin Držić, Široka 7, Dubrovnik, Croatia

curiosities:Ruđer Bošković.name: Ruđer Bošković
curiosities:Ruđer Bošković.teaser: A Jesuit from these lanes guessed in 1758 that matter is points held apart by forces
curiosities:Ruđer Bošković.story: Ruđer Josip Bošković was born in the Old Town on 18 May 1711, joined the Jesuits in Rome, and became one of the great scientific minds of his century: astronomer, mathematician, surveyor, diplomat for his Republic. His Theoria Philosophiae Naturalis, printed in Vienna in 1758, pictured matter not as hard little balls but as points with forces between them, repulsive up close and attractive further off. Two centuries later physicists recognised atomic and field ideas in it, and Heisenberg is credited with calling him the Croatian Leibniz. He was a Fellow of the Royal Society in London and died in Milan in 1787.
curiosities:Ruđer Bošković.why: Stand at the foot of the Jesuit Stairs: the square there carries his name.
facts: Poljana Ruđera Boškovića at the foot of the Jesuit Stairs, the steps Game of Thrones used for Cersei's walk

sources.label: MacTutor (St Andrews) — Boscovich, Dictionary of Scientific Biography

culture:The Rector's Palace.name: The Rector's Palace
culture:The Rector's Palace.teaser: A palace twice blown up by its own gunpowder, rebuilt with a Renaissance portico and a sailor's bust
culture:The Rector's Palace.story: The Republic kept its gunpowder in the building where it kept its head of state, and paid for it twice. An explosion in 1435 wrecked the old fortified residence; Onofrio della Cava, the Neapolitan who built the city's fountains, raised a late-Gothic palace in its place. A second blast in 1463 tore it again, and Michelozzo of Florence and Juraj Dalmatinac worked on the repair, which is why Gothic windows sit over a Renaissance portico of carved capitals. Inside the arcaded atrium stands the bust of Miho Pracat, the ship-owner from Lopud, the one private citizen the Republic honoured that way. Upstairs, the Cultural History Museum fills the state rooms.
culture:The Rector's Palace.why: Linger in the atrium: in summer it is one of the Festival's concert halls, and its acoustics are why.
facts: Pred Dvorom, between Luža square and the cathedral, Old Town
About 9am to 6pm April to October, 9am to 4pm November to March; closed Mondays in winter, and on 25 December, 1 January and 3 February (Oct 2026, reseller listing: confirm at the door)
About EUR 15 alone, or EUR 20 for the combined Dubrovnik Museums ticket covering ten sites, valid seven days (Oct 2026, reseller listing)
Opening time, before the tour groups
The portico capitals and the Pracat bust in the atrium

culture:Sponza and the Memorial Room.name: Sponza and the Memorial Room
culture:Sponza and the Memorial Room.teaser: The Republic weighed its trade in this courtyard; today one room holds the faces of those who defended it
culture:Sponza and the Memorial Room.story: Paskoje Miličević built the Sponza between 1516 and 1522 as the Republic's customs house, with its mint and treasury; every bale landed at the port passed under its arch, where a Latin line warns that the weights do not allow cheating, for God weighs with the weigher. It came through the 1667 quake and now keeps the Dubrovnik State Archives. In one wing is the Memorial Room of the Defenders: photographs of the men killed in the siege of 1991-92, which began on 1 October 1991. On 6 December 1991 alone the shelling killed 19 people and wounded 60. Most visitors pass in under a minute. Stay longer.
culture:Sponza and the Memorial Room.why: Read a few names and ages in the Memorial Room: most of them were barely twenty.
facts: Luža square, at the Ploče end of the Stradun
Memorial Room 9am to 9pm from 1 May to 31 October, 10am to 3pm in winter (Oct 2026)
Late afternoon, when the courtyard is quiet
The weights inscription on the courtyard arch, and copies of Archive documents on the ground floor (the Archives themselves are for researchers)

culture:Lazareti.name: Lazareti
culture:Lazareti.teaser: Ten stone halls outside Ploče Gate where caravans and their cargo waited out the plague before entering
culture:Lazareti.story: In 1377 Ragusa's Major Council made travellers from infected places wait outside the city before they entered. The halls beyond Ploče Gate came much later, dated 1627 by the World Monuments Fund and to work between about 1590 and 1642 by other accounts: a line of stone warehouses with walled yards where traders off the Ottoman roads, their goods and their animals sat out their days under guard. Today the halls are a cultural centre. In summer the Linđo Folklore Ensemble dances here under the vaults, a dance-master on the lijerica calling the steps. The season ended in early October.
culture:Lazareti.why: Come back in summer for a Linđo night: the old quarantine yard is the right stage for it.
facts: Frana Supila, just outside Ploče Gate
Event nights only; the 2026 Linđo season ran about 10 May to 10 October, Tuesdays and Fridays at 9.30pm by one listing (Oct 2026)
The walled yards between the halls, where the cargo was aired
